problem: The sentence says the 8086 drives 'RD or WR to set the direction of the transfer'. Direction is set by DT/R, as the previous sentence itself says. RD and WR only tell memory or I/O whether the cycle is a read or a write, so a student can end up with two conflicting rules for DT/R.
fix: Write: 'The 8086 drives M/IO to select memory or I/O, and RD or WR to say whether the cycle is a read or a write. DT/R alone sets the direction of the 8286: high for transmit, low for receive.'

where: Section 1 and Section 4 table, typical use
problem: The text says maximum mode 'exists for systems with a coprocessor, a DMA controller, or more than one bus master'. A single DMA controller can take the bus in minimum mode too, using HOLD and HLDA, so the rule as written is not a clean test between modes.
fix: Say maximum mode is needed when the board has a coprocessor or several bus masters that must arbitrate with RQ/GT and LOCK, or when the system wants the standard 8288 command set. A single DMA controller on a small board can still work in minimum mode through HOLD and HLDA.

problem: The arrow labelled 'timing' points from the 8086 to the 8284, which suggests the CPU feeds the clock generator. The 8284 supplies CLK, READY and RESET to the CPU.
fix: Reverse the edge so it runs from the 8284 node to the 8086 node, labelled 'CLK READY RESET'.

where: Figure (latch note and control bus note)
problem: The latch node is labelled 'A19-A16' and the edge from it to memory is labelled 'A19-A16', as if only the upper four address bits are latched; in fact two 8282 chips latch A0-A15 as well. The control bus node is labelled 'RD WR M/IO', which are minimum-mode names only.
fix: Label the latch node 'A0-A19, BHE' with the edge to memory labelled 'A0-A19, BHE', and label the control bus node 'MRDC MWTC IORC IOWC INTA (max) / RD WR M/IO (min)'.

problem: The text says the 8284 'divides the crystal frequency' but never gives the factor, which exam answers usually expect.
fix: Write: 'The 8284 divides the crystal frequency by 3 to produce CLK, so a 15 MHz crystal gives the 5 MHz clock the 8086 needs.'
